prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, based on magic-wavelength trapping of atoms, which brought time and frequency measurement to a fractional uncertainty of about 10^-18.

statement.case_for: I keep B010 with Katori and Ye as a single-part prize, and I have not changed my configuration since round 1. The test I apply first is independent confirmation, and the lattice clock passes it in a way few candidates do: strontium and ytterbium lattice clocks at JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE and NPL agree with each other at the 1e-18 level, and they are compared across continents. The systematic shifts (blackbody, lattice light shift, collisions) are individually measured and are explained by atomic-structure theory, which is the detailed calibration work I know from my own instruments. The two credits are distinct and decisive: Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and first demonstrations removed the trade-off between atom number and motional shifts, and Ye's group took it to record accuracy and into the many-body regime. On the chair's question about wording, I think the citation must name the magic-wavelength lattice scheme and the 1e-18 regime, because that is what separates this achievement from the 2005 comb prize (a counter for optical frequencies) and the 2012 ion-control prize (single-ion clocks). On the SI second, I would keep it out of the scientific case altogether. The science already stands without it: millimetre-scale gravitational time dilation, bounds on drifting constants and clock comparison over fibre and free space.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is still the one the committee has put to itself: B010 is a measurement capability more than the discovery of a new phenomenon, and it sits next to two earlier prizes in precision timekeeping. A committee that puts a discovery in nature first could reasonably prefer B061 or B051. The two-name credit leaves out Takamoto (first lattice-clock demonstration), Lemonde and the SYRTE group, Hollberg and the ion-clock groups, and the expert reports may weigh Katori's priority against Ye's accuracy record differently than we do. Five of eight round-1 configurations naming B010 is not independent evidence, because three of us moved there after the opening ballots, myself included. If an expert report shows that the 1e-18 claims depend on a single group's blackbody-shift evaluation, I would lower my confidence.

responses.point: Danielsson holds B061 first: the 2013 diffuse flux is the discovery, it has stood for more than a decade, and waiting for complete source identification would apply a stricter test than earlier prizes did. He asks for the reports to say who was decisive for the observation and wants independent confirmation weighed.
responses.response: I accept your timing argument. I do not think the diffuse flux is early, and I said so in round 1 and still believe it. My difficulty is about credit, and it is why I moved. A discovery by a collaboration of hundreds, with AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND as precursors, cannot be fairly split among three names unless the reports can point to who was decisive for the 2013 observation rather than for construction, and so far nobody, you included, has answered that. On independent confirmation, ANTARES and Baikal-GVD give consistent but weaker evidence, and KM3NeT is young, so most of the confirmation still rests on IceCube itself through different channels. Your question to Kroll about what the lattice clock has revealed that an earlier clock could not also deserves an answer from me: resolving gravitational redshift across a millimetre-scale sample and across a clock comparison network, and bounding a drift of constants at a level the earlier ion clocks could not reach. I would keep B061 as my first alternative and I would not oppose it if the reports resolve the attribution.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the earlier prizes did not contain the lattice idea, since the comb gave a frequency counter and the 2012 prize gave single-ion control, so the citation should be written around the lattice scheme. She also asks to keep the SI redefinition separate from the case.
responses.response: I agree on both points and my citation is written that way. It names magic-wavelength trapping and the 1e-18 regime and does not mention the second, so that the ion-clock and comb contributors are neither implicitly repeated nor implicitly excluded. The atomic-structure theory you describe is also the part I most need from a colleague. I cannot judge magic-wavelength calculations or blackbody-shift evaluations myself, but I can tell you that from the instrument side the proof is that independent apparatus with different systematics budgets agree. One caution: I would not write the theory into the citation as a separate credit, because that would open a third name we do not have on the list.

responses.point: Eriksson moved to B010 from B051 but does not accept that a measurement capability counts like a discovery, asks that the citation name the physics, and asks whether the 1e-18 claim is independent of blackbody-shift and lattice-light-shift systematics.
responses.response: The question about blackbody shifts is the right one and I will answer it as far as an instrument builder can. The 1e-18 level was reached in several independent clocks and checked in comparisons between strontium systems, with in-situ blackbody radiation thermometry and cryogenic operation, so I regard it as secure; I would still want the expert report to confirm it before the final ballot. On your first point, I would not call B010 a lesser kind of prize, since the discovery content is that a cold-atom ensemble can be controlled to a level where relativistic and many-body effects become routine measurements. Your B051 alternative is still there, and I do not think you should vote for B010 only because the majority is there. I would be satisfied if you voted for it on the physics.

responses.point: Kroll names Takamoto's 2005 demonstration and the SYRTE work as real contributions outside the credited names, but argues that they do not displace the distinct proposals and records of Katori and Ye. He regards B041 as less urgent because of the 2025 circuit prize.
responses.response: I accept your reading of Takamoto and SYRTE, and I will not pretend they are not contributions. Takamoto, working in Katori's group, demonstrated the first lattice clock, so under any credit rule the Katori credit includes that demonstration, which is a reason for the citation to say invention and realisation. Lemonde's contribution is more difficult, and I would ask the reports whether it is a rival priority claim or a parallel development. You also raised the Kimble-era magic-wavelength discussion; I think that is a weaker rival claim than Katori's, because the proposal that was made quantitative and realised was his. On B041, your adjacency point against my own Wallraff-Blais-Schoelkopf interest is fair, and it is not one of my alternatives.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B039 for aberration-corrected electron microscopy as an instrument that broke the Scherzer limit, with a compact three-person credit, and she discloses field proximity and says she would not insist if a fair prize cannot be built from those three names.
responses.response: I like the Scherzer argument as an instrument builder, and it was my own fourth-ranked candidate. But your own conditions are the weakness. The TEM corrector credit (Rose, Haider, Urban) is separate from the STEM corrector line (Krivanek, Dellby), and a three-name prize that omits one line invites the objection you already raise. I think the lattice clock stands on firmer ground, because both of its named contributions are decisive and neither of the other main lines is excluded in the same way. I also welcome your disclosure of field proximity. I would not ask you to recuse for an alternative, but I would discount B039 support as you propose.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B047 for the quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators, with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, a clean mechanism, a complete theory-to-experiment chain and an HgTe realisation, but concedes the allocation omits Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and Hasan and that the 2016 prize may make it look redundant.
responses.response: You make the best case for a discovery in nature among the condensed-matter candidates, and I admit the HgTe experiment is the kind of decisive confirmation I respect. My objection is the same as yours: any three names leave out the BHZ prediction or the 3D ARPES line, and the 2016 prize makes the committee's second topological award hard to defend as urgent. If the committee prefers a mechanism over a capability, I think B047 is the better of the condensed-matter options, and B051 depends on a pairing mechanism that is still not understood. I could not support B047 over B010 on current attribution, but I would listen if you tell me how the credit among Kane, Mele and Molenkamp would be made unambiguous.

uncertainties: Whether the expert reports confirm that the 1e-18 uncertainty is independent of a single group's blackbody-shift and lattice-light-shift evaluation, and how they weigh Katori's proposal against Takamoto, Lemonde and SYRTE.
Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes if the citation names the magic-wavelength scheme and the 1e-18 regime.
Whether the reports can identify who among Halzen, Karle and Spiering was decisive for the 2013 IceCube observation, which would change my view of B061 as the main alternative.
Whether a measurement capability is weighted the same as a discovery in nature by the full committee, since I know I may be giving that point extra weight for B010 as an instrument builder.
statement.conflict_note: I have no apparent conflict for B010: I am not connected to Katori, Ye, RIKEN or JILA that I can identify from my profile. For B061 I work in astroparticle physics at KTH and belong to the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations, not IceCube as far as my profile shows, and I have moved to B010 partly so that my field affinity does not decide the outcome; B061 remains an alternative, so the committee may wish to weigh my view on it with that in mind. I flag B012 and B057 only as shared detector expertise. As chair I also note that I wrote the round 1 summary, and have tried to describe positions as members stated them.
